# Sarabhaṅgajātaka (Ja 522)

**ID:** Ja 522  
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Sarabhaṅgajātaka  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul0.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul0.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sarabhaṅgajātaka* (Ja 522) is a birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection within the Khuddaka Nikāya [Appleton 2010]. According to the narrative frame, the Buddha related this story while dwelling at the Bamboo Grove concerning the death of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna [Keown 1996]. In the core legend, the Bodhisatta was born as the archer Jotipāla (later the sage Sarabhaṅga), renowned for his exceptional archery feats—such as shooting an iron arrow to defend against four archers, a display of martial arts referred to elsewhere in the Pali *Nidānakathā* to illustrate the Buddha's own youth [Murphy 2010; Gombrich 1991; Gaffney 2003; Fausböll 1897]. Later as the teacher Sarabhaṅga, he responds to doctrinal and moral inquiries posed by deities including Sakka, discoursing on patience with rough speech, the definition of the virtuous person (*sappurisa*), and the nature of the truly wise person [Anandajoti 2010]. In Jātakapāḷi editorial structure, Ja 522 is notable for including a verse connection (*samodhāna*) identifying the Buddha with the title *lokanātha* rather than using the standard term *bodhisatta* [Appleton 2010].

 Scenes depicting the Bodhisatta Jotipāla's archery feat from the *Sarabhaṅgajātaka* have also been identified in Southeast Asian art, notably on 7th–12th-century Dvaravati Buddhist boundary markers (*sīmā*) from the Khorat Plateau [Murphy 2010].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: San Lo Mvu 99 The Jātaka of Śarabhaṅga
- Passage-level parallels: SN 11.9 Araññāyatanaisisutta

**Sources**

- [Murphy 2010] Stephen A. Murphy, Buddhist Boundary Markers of Northeast Thailand and Central Laos, 7th-12th C. Khorat Plateau — Discusses artistic depictions of Jotipāla defending against four archers on Khorat Plateau sīmā stones.
- [Gombrich 1991] Richard F. Gombrich, Buddhist Precept and Practice: Traditional Buddhism in Rural Highlands of Ceylon (1991) — Notes the Nidānakathā's reference to the Sarabhaṅgajātaka for the feat-of-arms episode.
- [Anandajoti 2010] Bhikkhu Ānandajoti, Buddhist Wisdom Verses: 551 verses from the Canon (2010) — Quotes and outlines verses from Ja 522 concerning Sakka's questions on virtue, patience with rough speech, and wisdom.
- [Appleton 2010] Naomi Appleton, Jātaka Stories in Theravāda Buddhism: Narrating the Bodhisatta Path (2010) — Examines canonical classification and notes that the verse samodhāna in Ja 522 designates the protagonist as lokanātha.
- [Fausböll 1897] V. Fausböll, The Jātaka Together with Its Commentary, Vol. 7 (1897) — Supplies index and character details identifying Sarabhaṅga as Jotipālakumāra.
- [Gaffney 2003] Sean D. Gaffney, The Jātakanidānakathā: A Critical Study (2003) — Documents the Nidānakathā citing the Sarabhaṅgajātaka for the Bodhisatta's exhibition of archery arts.
- [Keown 1996] Damien Keown, Karma, Character, and Consequentialism (1996) — Mentions the introductory story to Ja 522 explaining Moggallāna's death and karma.
- [Norman 1997] K.R. Norman, A Philological Approach to Buddhism (1997) — Identifies the Sarabhaṅga-jātaka as a shared narrative found in both Theravāda and the Mahāvastu.
